ergonomic-workspace-assessment.title: Audit Workspace Friction Before Buying More Gear
ergonomic-workspace-assessment.subtitle: Change the layout around the task, one reversible step at a time.
ergonomic-workspace-assessment.description: Inspect where a workspace makes the actual task harder to see, reach, switch, connect, or reset; change one layout variable; and keep the change only when it removes friction without creating a new problem.
ergonomic-workspace-assessment.reason: Replace unsupported productivity and discomfort outcomes, pseudo-medical posture rules, rigid dimensions and timing prescriptions, and fabricated observations with a bounded workspace-friction audit.

lifeOsSource.hack: Design the workspace around the work you actually do: find one recurring reach, visibility, glare, cable, switching, or setup problem and change that variable before buying more equipment.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Choose one frequent task, walk through it slowly, note every unnecessary reach, obstruction, visibility issue, cable move, device swap, or reset, rank the friction points, change one reversible layout variable, use the task again, and keep or undo the change based on what became easier or harder.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which step in the task had avoidable friction, what single workspace change did I make, and did it remove that friction without moving the problem somewhere else?

faq.question: Do I need to buy ergonomic equipment first?
faq.answer: No. Start by observing the task and the current layout. Moving a monitor, relocating a frequently used device, routing a cable, or clearing a reach path may solve the actual friction without a purchase.

faq.question: Is this a guide for treating pain or preventing injury?
faq.answer: No. This protocol is about workspace layout and task friction. Persistent pain, numbness, weakness, or other health concerns belong with an appropriate workplace or health professional rather than this checklist.

intro.html: A workspace can look organized and still make the real job awkward. Review it as a small system: task, person, tools, information, cables, surfaces, light, and handoffs. The useful question is not whether the setup looks ergonomic; it is where the task repeatedly becomes harder than it needs to be.

sections.title: 1. Choose one frequent task
sections.html: Pick a task you repeat: writing, reviewing a document, joining calls, comparing two screens, drawing, packing, testing hardware, or another routine. Define its start and finish so the workspace can be judged against a concrete job.

sections.title: 2. Trace the task and mark friction
sections.html: Perform the task slowly. Note unnecessary reaching, repeated window or device switching, blocked sightlines, glare, loose cables, items that must be moved twice, missing charging access, or tools that live outside the natural work area. Record what happens rather than guessing what the ideal setup should be.

sections.title: 3. Change one reversible variable
sections.html: Move one object, change one screen position, relocate one frequently used tool, reroute one cable, or create one dedicated place for an item. Prefer changes that are easy to undo so cause and effect remain visible.

sections.title: 4. Run the task again
sections.html: Repeat the same task and compare the troublesome step. Keep the change if the task is simpler and no important new problem appears. Undo or revise it when the friction merely moved elsewhere. Buy equipment only when the remaining constraint is clear enough to name.

affirmation-habit-tracker.title: Write an Affirmation You Can Actually Act On
affirmation-habit-tracker.subtitle: Replace grand claims with a grounded statement and one next action.
affirmation-habit-tracker.description: Turn a vague positive statement into words you can presently stand behind, connect it to one action under your control, and revise the statement when it becomes false, empty, or unhelpful.
affirmation-habit-tracker.reason: Replace therapy-adjacent framing, unsupported behavioral outcomes, fabricated first-party observations, rigid repetition schedules, and selectively presented literature claims with a bounded statement-to-action exercise.

lifeOsSource.hack: If an affirmation sounds false or grandiose, rewrite it as a grounded statement about a value, intention, capability, or next action you can honestly endorse today.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Write the positive statement you are tempted to use, underline the part that feels exaggerated or outside your control, replace it with language you can currently stand behind, attach one concrete action that would be consistent with the statement, and review the wording after you act.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Can I honestly endorse this statement now, what action does it point to, and should I keep, narrow, or replace the wording after seeing what I actually did?

faq.question: What if an affirmation feels fake?
faq.answer: Do not force it. Narrow the wording until it describes something you can honestly endorse, such as an intention, a value, a capability you are developing, or one action you control.

faq.question: Do I have to repeat the statement a fixed number of times?
faq.answer: No. This protocol does not depend on a repetition count. The useful output is a credible statement connected to an action, followed by a check of whether the wording still fits reality.

intro.html: Positive language becomes less useful when it asks you to pretend. A stronger version is grounded: it says something you can presently endorse and points toward behavior you control. The statement is a prompt for action, not a claim that words alone change circumstances.

sections.title: 1. Write the statement you want to believe
sections.html: Start with the natural version, even when it is broad: I am confident, I finish what I start, or I can handle this. Then ask which words describe reality and which words are doing wishful work.

sections.title: 2. Ground it in something you control
sections.html: Replace absolute identity language with a value, intention, current capability, or next behavior. For example, I am always confident can become I can prepare one clear point and say it when the opportunity appears.

sections.title: 3. Attach one next action
sections.html: Choose a small action that would make the statement more concrete: draft the point, send the message, open the document, ask the question, or schedule the task. The action should remain useful even if the statement does not change how you feel.

sections.title: 4. Revise from reality
sections.html: After acting, read the statement again. Keep it if it remains honest and useful. Narrow it when it overreaches; replace it when another statement would better describe the next decision. There is no need to defend wording that no longer fits.

coot-ai-growth-journal.title: Turn an AI Reflection into One Next Action
coot-ai-growth-journal.subtitle: Use the model to structure options; keep the decision and verification with you.
coot-ai-growth-journal.description: Give an AI assistant a concrete goal, current constraints, and the decision you need to make; ask for options, assumptions, and failure modes; verify factual claims; then choose one reversible next action yourself.
coot-ai-growth-journal.reason: Replace obsolete Coot.AI branding, fabricated completion-rate observations, pseudo-optimized session lengths, mental-health-adjacent language, and unsupported follow-through claims with a vendor-neutral AI reflection and decision protocol.

lifeOsSource.hack: Use an AI conversation to make a decision surface explicit: goal, constraints, options, assumptions, risks, missing information, and one next action. Do not outsource the final judgment or factual verification.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: State one concrete goal or decision, provide the relevant constraints and what you already know, ask the AI for a small set of distinct options with assumptions and failure modes, challenge anything vague, verify factual claims that matter, choose one reversible next action yourself, and record what would cause you to change course.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: What became clearer, which AI claim still needs verification, what action did I choose, and what new information would make me revise the decision?

faq.question: Should I ask the AI to choose for me?
faq.answer: Use it to expose options, assumptions, trade-offs, and missing information. Keep the final decision with the person who owns the consequences, especially when the choice is costly, irreversible, or high stakes.

faq.question: What should I verify before acting?
faq.answer: Verify factual claims that materially affect the decision, including dates, prices, rules, technical constraints, external commitments, and other information the model could have misunderstood or invented.

intro.html: An AI conversation is most useful here as a decision workspace rather than an authority. Bring one concrete goal, enough context to expose the real constraints, and a clear request for alternatives. The session should end with a decision you own, a fact-check list, and one next action.

sections.title: 1. Frame one decision
sections.html: Write what you are trying to accomplish, what has already happened, what cannot change, what resources are available, and what decision is currently blocking progress. Avoid asking a broad question when a narrower decision is available.

sections.title: 2. Ask for distinct options and failure modes
sections.html: Ask for a small number of meaningfully different approaches. For each, request the main assumption, trade-off, likely failure mode, and information that would distinguish it from the alternatives. Reject lists that are merely paraphrases of the same plan.

sections.title: 3. Separate reasoning from facts
sections.html: Mark statements that depend on external facts and verify the ones that could change the decision. For high-stakes legal, financial, medical, safety, or security questions, use appropriate qualified sources rather than treating model output as sufficient authority.

sections.title: 4. Choose one reversible next action
sections.html: Select the smallest useful action that either creates progress or generates information. Record what you chose, why, and what signal would cause you to stop, revise, or choose another option. The AI can help structure the record; responsibility for the action remains with you.
